Hormuz: Iran says it sank a supertanker carrying 2 million barrels, but oil slips at the open as markets wait for proof

On Sunday, November 15, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed that a supertanker carrying more than 2 million barrels had sunk after hitting a mine in the Strait of Hormuz. No one has confirmed it. Yet on Monday morning in Asia, Brent fell 0.5% to $95.37 a barrel [1][2][4].

According to a Revolutionary Guards statement read on state television, “two oil tankers taking an unauthorized route in the southern Strait of Hormuz struck naval mines, causing powerful explosions and a fire” [1][2].

“One of these vessels, a supertanker carrying more than two million barrels of crude, sank in the waters of the southern Persian Gulf,” the statement added. Neither the name, the flag nor the owner of the ships was given [1][3].
On Sunday evening, the Iranian navy announced that another tanker was on fire after hitting a mine east of the strait, according to state media; Reuters was unable to verify the report [5].
The UK Maritime Trade Operations center (UKMTO) said the crew of one of the ships was safe, but that the damage and the environmental impact remained unknown [3].
Since Saturday, the US military has disputed Iran's account of three tankers hit by mines; it says it has cleared the main routes of mines [6][7].
On Monday at around 2:45 a.m. (Paris time), Brent was down 47 cents at $95.37, and US crude WTI was down 23 cents at $88.33, according to Reuters [4].
Since the war began in late February, Iran has required ships to use routes it authorizes, and at least 25 sailors have died in and around the strait, according to the UN [2][8].

The key takeaway: the war of words around Hormuz no longer moves prices. A sunken supertanker holding 2 million barrels would normally be a shock; this time, the price of oil is falling, because traders want independent confirmation after a series of unverifiable Iranian announcements in recent weeks [1][5].

The market is mainly watching supply. According to Reuters, shipments through Hormuz have almost returned to their pre-war level, and the International Energy Agency said on Friday that global supply exceeded demand for the first time since the conflict began [4][5].

For Tehran, these announcements serve a purpose: to remind everyone that the southern route, the one protected by the US Navy, remains dangerous, and to deter shipowners and insurers. Iran says it has hit four ships in total, a figure no outside authority has confirmed [3][7].

If a sinking were confirmed, analysts see a risk of a rapid rise: an oil spill of that size would close part of the Gulf and drive up insurance premiums, and therefore the cost of shipping oil to Asia and Europe [6][7].

For now, oil is staying around $95 a barrel and is not soaring: the cost of filling your tank shouldn't change this week because of this announcement. But if a sinking is confirmed, oil could gain several dollars within hours, and pump prices follow within one to two weeks, especially for diesel.

China: retail sales grow just 0.4% in October and investment plunges 8.1%, three days before the summit with Trump and Putin

On Monday, November 16, China's National Bureau of Statistics released October figures that all fell short of expectations: retail sales up just 0.4% year on year, industrial output up 4.8%, and investment down 8.1% over ten months, dragged down by real estate (−21.6%) [1][2][3].
Retail sales, the best gauge of household consumption, rose only 0.4% year on year in October, compared with 1.1% in September; economists had expected 0.8% [1][8].
In detail, sales of goods gained just 0.3% and catering 0.7%, even though October included the National Day holiday week and the start of the “Singles' Day” sales [8][9].
Factory output slowed to 4.8% year on year, after 5.5% in September, while forecasts had pointed to around 5.3% [1][2].

Fixed-asset investment (factories, roads, housing) fell 8.1% over the first ten months of the year, worse than the expected −7% and the −7.2% recorded at the end of September; Bloomberg Línea calls it a record low [3][5].
Real estate remains the big black hole: developer investment plunged 21.6%, housing starts 24.4%, home sales 14.1% and funds raised by developers 21.9% [3].
Private investment fell 11.4%, and investment by state-controlled companies 4%: it is not only developers who are pulling back [3].
New home prices fell another 0.1% in a month and 2.4% in a year; only 21 of the 70 major cities tracked saw prices stabilize or rise [4][10].

The key takeaway: the Chinese economy is holding up thanks to its exports, but domestic demand is running out of steam. Households are spending barely more than a year ago, and companies are investing less and less [1][3][5].

Beijing has set a growth target of 4.5% to 5% for 2026, announced on March 5 by Premier Li Qiang before the National People's Congress [6]. In the third quarter, GDP grew 4.5% year on year, and 4.6% over nine months: just above the bottom of the range, and mostly thanks to export-oriented factories [7].
Yet economists do not expect a new stimulus plan before the end of the year. For ING economist Lynn Song, 2026 will remain one of the weakest years for Chinese domestic demand in a long time [1][2].

The timing makes these figures sensitive: on Thursday, November 19, Xi Jinping is due to host Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, on the sidelines of the APEC summit [11]. A China that consumes little seeks to sell more abroad, which fuels trade tensions with Washington and Brussels.

When Chinese people buy less at home, their factories sell their products elsewhere, especially in Europe: electric cars, solar panels and machinery arrive at rock-bottom prices. That is good news for your wallet, but a threat to European industry, and the reason Brussels keeps launching investigations and imposing tariffs.

Czechia: between 350,000 and 450,000 people in Prague protest against putting public TV and radio on the state budget, Babiš refuses to back down

On Sunday, November 15, hundreds of thousands of Czechs filled the Letná Plain in Prague to protest Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's plan to abolish the license fee and fund public television and radio from the state budget. Babiš acknowledges the right to protest, but is sticking with his bill [1][2][3].

The rally was organized by the association A Million Moments for Democracy. Its main organizer, Mikuláš Minář, puts the turnout at 350,000; the organizers claim up to 450,000 participants, and Euronews cites 350,000 to 400,000 based on Czech media [1][2][5].
It would be the largest protest in the history of independent Czechia, born in 1993. The rally was peaceful, according to the police [1][5].
The disputed bill abolishes the license fee paid by households and replaces it with funding from the state budget for Czech Television (ČT) and Czech Radio (ČRo) [2][3].
The protesters also called on Andrej Babiš to dismiss the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Tomio Okamura, and to take the Defense Ministry away from his far-right party [2].
Employees of the two public broadcasters had already gone on strike against the plan before the rally [6]. Opposition leaders joined the crowd at Letná [4].
The date had been set after a first protest on October 25, two days before November 17, the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution [7].
In March 2026, the same movement had already gathered around 250,000 people at Letná against the Babiš government [8].

The key takeaway: for opponents, a public broadcaster paid directly from the budget depends each year on the goodwill of the government, which can threaten it with cuts. The license fee, by contrast, gives it its own income. That financial link is what the Letná crowd is defending [1][2].
Andrej Babiš rejects these arguments. “Nobody wants to nationalize them,” he told Czech Television, and he promises to keep backing the bill in its second and then third reading in Parliament [2].

The standoff goes beyond the media: the protesters are also targeting the Prime Minister's far-right allies, including Tomio Okamura. For the opposition, which turned out in force at Letná, the public media reform is part of the same logic of “government by force” denounced by the protesters [2][4].

The A Million Moments for Democracy movement is no newcomer: it has filled Letná during every major crisis for years, and this time it confronted the government with record mobilization, two days before the November 17 national holiday [7][8].

France no longer has a license fee either, and the question of how to fund public broadcasting regularly comes back in its budgets. What is at stake in Prague concerns all of Europe: who holds the purse strings of a public newsroom, and what they can do with them. A Czechia tearing itself apart is also one more partner weighing on European decisions, which are often taken unanimously.

Russian shadow fleet: European troops board a tanker under a false flag in the Mediterranean, ahead of 145 new sanctions this Monday

On Sunday, November 15, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas announced that the European naval mission Irini had inspected the tanker MV Midag in the Mediterranean on November 13; the vessel is suspected of belonging to the Russian shadow fleet and was sailing under a false flag. European ministers are due to adopt new sanctions this Monday [1][2][3].
The boarding was carried out by the European operation EUNAVFOR MED Irini. It confirmed that the MV Midag was sailing under a false flag, Kaja Kallas wrote on X [1][3].
The tracking site MarineTraffic showed the vessel flying the flag of Zimbabwe; that is the flag the European troops deemed false during the inspection [2].

The inspection is based on Article 110 of the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, which allows a warship to board, on the high seas, a vessel suspected of having no nationality or of falsely flying a flag [3][6].
This Monday, November 16, EU foreign ministers are due to approve new additions to the sanctions list, targeting banks, buyers and companies that help the shadow fleet, according to Kaja Kallas [3].

On November 11, the ambassadors of the 27 member states agreed on 145 entities and individuals, including 50 Russian banks, shadow fleet intermediaries and energy groups; the measures take effect as soon as they are published [4].
European Commissioner Maria Luís Albuquerque said these lists also target Russian oil refineries [5].
Moscow rejects the accusations about its shadow fleet, a “political fabrication” according to the Russian Foreign Ministry [2].

The key takeaway: the “shadow fleet” is made up of hundreds of old tankers with opaque owners that carry Russian oil despite the price cap and Western sanctions. By stopping them at sea and sanctioning those who finance them, the EU is trying to cut the oil revenue that pays for the war in Ukraine [1][4].

Europe is moving from blacklists to action at sea. In March 2026, the Irini mission was given the right to board vessels suspected of falsely flying a flag; since then it has inspected several tankers, including the Sun on August 30 [6][7].
Targeting 50 banks at once means going after the financial plumbing: without a bank to pay for insurance, freight or the cargo, oil is harder to sell, or sells at a steeper discount [4].

The EU promises to continue “at sea and through diplomatic channels,” Kaja Kallas said. The risk is escalation: each boarding could provoke a Russian response, while the Mediterranean is a major route for oil [1][3].

Less Russian oil sold under the radar means less money for the Russian army, but also slightly fewer barrels on the world market. With Brent already around $96 because of Hormuz, every turn of the screw can weigh marginally on what you pay to fill your tank.

Civil servants: 1.35 million of the lowest-paid public employees will get extra index points, for just over €1 billion, but no across-the-board raise

On Sunday, November 15, on franceinfo, David Amiel, Minister for the Civil Service, confirmed an increase in index points for the lowest-paid public employees: with the rise in the Smic minimum wage, 1.35 million employees will be affected, at a cost of just over €1 billion. The value of the index point itself remains frozen [1][2].
“There will indeed be an increase in points for the lowest salaries in the civil service,” said David Amiel, a guest on franceinfo's 8.30 program [1].
The measure will affect 1.35 million employees, taking into account the increase in the Smic, and will cost just over €1 billion, according to the minister [1].
The government still rules out a general increase in the index point, which is used to calculate the base pay of all civil servants; its last increase was three years ago [2].
Last week, Sébastien Lecornu offered the unions a month of talks, notably on “raising low salaries” in the civil service [1].

On November 9, after the social conference at Matignon, the government brought forward to December 1 the 1.6% increase in the Smic, which will rise from about €1,478 to about €1,502 net per month for a full-time job [3][4].
This increase combines the automatic raise of about 1% planned for January, brought forward by a month, and a boost of about 0.6 points decided by the government [3][4].

These announcements come as the state budget was rejected on November 4 in the National Assembly and the Senate is examining the Social Security budget until November 18, then the state budget from November 20 [5][6][7].

The key takeaway: when the Smic rises, the lowest steps of the civil service pay scale risk falling below the minimum wage. The state then has to add index points at the bottom of the scale, otherwise a category C employee would earn less than a private-sector worker on the Smic [1][3].

The government is opting for a targeted increase because a general rise in the index point would cost far more: it would benefit all employees, not just the 1.35 million at the bottom of the scale [1][2]. With a public deficit that the Senate wants to bring down to 5% of GDP in 2027, Matignon is hunting for every euro [2][5].

It is also a response to anger over the cost of living: the unions are demanding more both for the Smic and for civil servants, and the government still refuses to unfreeze the index point for everyone [2][3].

The bill adds to a budget with no majority: after the unanimous rejection of the revenue section in the National Assembly on November 4, the government's original text went to the Senate, and the executive could resort to Article 49.3 or to ordinances if Parliament does not decide by December 17 [6][7].

If you work on the Smic, your December paycheck will rise by about €20 net for a full-time job. If you are a public employee at the bottom of the scale (category C), you should gain a few index points; above that, your base pay won't change as long as the index point stays frozen.

United States: after skies were closed for nearly five hours, Trump demands $50 billion “fast” for air traffic control, Democrats cry “ransom”

After all takeoffs in the United States were halted on Friday, November 13, due to a communications outage, Donald Trump asked Congress on Sunday to “give the money, fast.” His administration is seeking $50 billion to overhaul air traffic control; Democrats point out that funds approved in 2025 have not been spent [1][2][3].

On Friday, November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) banned all departures in the country from about 3:54 p.m. to 8:15 p.m. Washington time, after an outage in communications between controllers and aircraft [4][5].
Cancellations lasted all weekend: more than 5,900 flights canceled and more than 7,000 delayed on Saturday alone, according to Yahoo News [5].

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blames a router installed in El Dorado, Arkansas, during work by the company L3Harris: it allegedly “flooded” the network with connection requests. L3Harris says it is cooperating with the investigation; the routers have been sent to its headquarters in Florida for testing [5][6].
FAA chief Bryan Bedford says he has “no evidence” of a malicious act [4].

On Friday evening, Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin asked Congress for $50 billion, a day after a formal request for $30.1 billion made with budget director Russ Vought [1][7].
On Sunday, Donald Trump wrote on his social network that he had a plan, but that Congress had to “give the money, FAST!”, and he blamed Joe Biden [1][8].
On the other side, Democratic lawmakers Rick Larsen and André Carson are asking why the FAA needs more when unspent funds remain; Rosa DeLauro calls it a “ransom” [3].

The key takeaway: a single faulty piece of equipment was enough to ground the world's leading aviation power. The outage highlights an aging air traffic control system, which Sean Duffy describes with its “old switches” and “little copper lines from the 1980s” [1][4].

The battle is now over the budget. In July 2025, Congress had already approved $12.5 billion to modernize air traffic control, a “down payment” according to Duffy, who says the money will be spent by the end of 2028 [1]. The administration is now asking for four times as much, and Democrats first want to know where the funds already approved stand [1][3].

Explanations also differ within the administration: Duffy blames old equipment, while Markwayne Mullin speaks of a “patchwork” modernization that allegedly overloaded the older equipment. A report by the GAO, Congress's watchdog, had already criticized the FAA in September 2026 for lacking a full cost estimate and an overall schedule for this work [1].
The economic cost is heavy: hundreds of thousands of travelers stranded, cargo flights delayed, college football games postponed, and a secretary who refuses to apologize for halting flights [5][9].

If you need to travel to the United States or connect through it in the coming weeks, leave yourself some margin: until the network is repaired, another outage remains possible, Sean Duffy himself warned. And Europe is not immune: its own air traffic control systems are aging too.

Ukraine: Zelensky says SpaceX's throttling of Starshield terminals is opening the skies to Russian drones targeting energy before winter

On Sunday, November 15, after a night of Russian strikes on energy and rail in eight regions, Volodymyr Zelensky claimed that the speed limit imposed on SpaceX's Starshield satellite terminals is preventing his interceptor drones from catching Russian drones. SpaceX denies any change [1][2][3].

According to Kyiv, Starshield terminals, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink network, no longer work above about 161 km/h: Ukrainian interceptor drones lose their connection at high speed and can no longer catch up with Russian Shahed-type drones [4][5].
Ukrainian officials date this throttling to October 14; on October 24, Zelensky had announced a return to normal, before saying the limits had come back [4].
Overnight from Saturday to Sunday, Russia struck energy and railway infrastructure in eight regions; in Chornomorsk, a port in the Odesa region, six people were injured [2].
The Ukrainian military says it shot down 106 of the 132 drones launched overnight; an energy facility hit in the Odesa region left 41,000 households without power [1].
Zelensky says he has tasked the foreign and defense ministries and his office with resolving the issue with Washington and SpaceX, and doubts it is a mere technical problem [4][6].

SpaceX told the website Axios that these accusations were “false” and that there had “been no change”; according to the Wall Street Journal, it was Elon Musk who ordered the restrictions, and Donald Trump denies that the White House requested them [4].

The key takeaway: a private American company holds part of Ukraine's air defense in its hands. Cheap interceptor drones have become a key weapon against Russian Shaheds, and they rely on SpaceX satellites to be piloted [4][5].

Winter is what's at stake. Moscow is targeting the power grid and the railways to deprive Ukrainians of heating and disrupt the economy; every drone that gets through can cut power to tens of thousands of households, as in the Odesa region [1][2].

The issue is also diplomatic. Zelensky recalls that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had assured him that Starshield was more under the US government's control; yet Washington-led peace negotiations are under way, and Kyiv suspects pressure [4][6].

The affair raises a question for Kyiv's allies, Europeans included: can military communications be entrusted to a private network? Zelensky stresses that the decision to throttle the terminals appears to come from SpaceX itself, despite US assurances, and that the company denies any change [4][6].

A Ukraine plunged into darkness means more emergency aid for the EU to fund, and therefore your taxes, and more risk for electricity prices in Eastern Europe. It is also a concrete reminder: the satellites of a handful of private companies now weigh on wars.

Francophonie: in Phnom Penh, Macron asked Kagame to withdraw the Rwandan candidate, Kigali refuses and Kinshasa threatens to walk out

The 20th Francophonie Summit opened on Sunday, November 15, in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, in the presence of Emmanuel Macron. This Monday it is due to elect the Secretary-General of the OIF, in a vote torn by the rivalry between DR Congo and Rwanda, whose candidate Louise Mushikiwabo is seeking a third term [1][2][4].

The summit is being held on November 15 and 16; it is the first time Cambodia has hosted it, and France is due to hand over to it the presidency of the International Organization of La Francophonie [1][6].
Four candidates are running for the 2027-2030 term: Rwanda's Louise Mushikiwabo, the outgoing Secretary-General, Congo's Juliana Lumumba, Romania's Dacian Cioloș and Mauritania's Coumba Ba [4].
For the first time, the election will not be decided by consensus but by secret ballot, among the 53 full member states and governments [4][5].
According to Kigali, Emmanuel Macron asked President Paul Kagame to withdraw Louise Mushikiwabo's candidacy; Rwanda refused. DR Congo is threatening to leave the OIF if she is re-elected [1].
The Élysée says most members want a consensus and that the president will discuss it with his African counterparts [1][2].
Having arrived on Saturday, Emmanuel Macron is making Cambodia the first stop on a tour of Southeast Asia; he is due to meet Prime Minister Hun Manet and sign about ten agreements [2].
Also expected are Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Vietnamese leader Tô Lâm, Paul Kagame and Congolese President Félix Tshisekedi [1].

The key takeaway: the election of the Secretary-General has become a battleground of the war in eastern DR Congo. Kinshasa, the United States and UN experts accuse Rwanda of backing the M23 rebels, which Kigali denies; voting for or against the Rwandan candidate amounts to taking sides [1].

The rivalry goes back a while: the Congolese government put forward Juliana Lumumba as early as February 26, 2026, to block Louise Mushikiwabo [7]. The secret ballot, a first, makes the outcome uncertain [4][5].
For Paris, the goal is to avoid an organization split in two: a departure by DR Congo, as Kinshasa threatens, would weaken La Francophonie just as France hands over its presidency to Cambodia [1][3].
The summit also serves as an economic showcase: Macron's tour of Southeast Asia aims at agreements with countries seeking partners between China and the United States [2][3].

La Francophonie may seem far away, but it has 53 full members and serves France as a network of influence, especially in Africa. An organization tearing itself apart means less weight for Paris in countries where access to minerals is at stake, such as the Congolese cobalt in your batteries.

Japan: the economy shrinks for the first time in a year, squeezed between expensive oil, a weak yen and an earthquake in Kumamoto

On Monday, November 16, the Japanese government announced that GDP had fallen 0.1% at an annualized rate between July and September, the first decline in four quarters. Economists had expected growth of 0.2%. Household consumption is falling, and the bill for imported oil is swelling [1][2][4].
According to the Cabinet Office's preliminary estimate, real GDP fell 0.02% from the previous quarter, or −0.1% at an annualized rate [1][3][4].
The average forecast of 13 financial institutions surveyed by the government had pointed to growth of 0.2% at an annualized rate [4].

Household consumption, more than half of the economy, fell 0.3% over the quarter, its second straight decline, hurt by the high cost of living, difficult weather and the magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture in late July [4][5].
Imports jumped 2.5%, inflated by energy prices, while exports fell 0.2%: foreign trade therefore dragged growth down [5].

The only real bright spot, business investment rose 1.6% over the quarter, or 6.8% at an annualized rate according to AP, driven by digital demand; residential investment, on the other hand, fell 1.1% [2][4].
In nominal terms, that is, without stripping out price increases, GDP grew 1.6% at an annualized rate [4].
This decline follows three quarters of modest growth: in the spring, the economy had grown 1.4% at an annualized rate, according to the revised estimate in September [2][6].

The key takeaway: Japan is paying a high price for the Hormuz crisis. The country imports almost all of its oil, and the main route for that oil, the Strait of Hormuz, is virtually blocked, AP notes. The energy bill is climbing, and households are cutting back on other spending [2].

The weak yen makes the problem worse: with the dollar at around 160 yen, every barrel paid for in dollars costs the Japanese more [2]. It is a vicious circle: expensive oil widens the trade deficit, which weighs further on the currency.

The decline remains minimal, almost stagnation, and business investment shows that industry is still betting on the future, particularly in digital [2][4]. But it complicates the Bank of Japan's task: raising rates to support the yen would risk further slowing an economy that is stalling.
This is a preliminary estimate: the figure will be revised on December 8, and it could swing either way, as in the spring, when growth was revised upward [6][7].

Japan is a major supplier to Europe (cars, machinery, components). A slowing Japan and a weak yen make its products cheaper to export, which puts pressure on European manufacturers. And it is a reminder that the Hormuz blockade weighs on every economy that imports its oil, including France.

news.2026-11-16-canada-carney-constructe: Autos: Mark Carney warns that Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Trump fail

On a tour of Asia, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Saturday and Sunday that his country would not accept any deal with the United States without a viable Canadian auto industry, and that otherwise its factories could take in Chinese investment. He is due to discuss it with Xi Jinping in Shenzhen this week [1][2][3].

Speaking in Manila, Mark Carney said: “This government will not settle for a deal with the United States that is not compatible with a viable Canadian auto sector”; a bilateral deal is “possible, but we're not there yet” [2][4].

Canadian cars currently face 25% tariffs to enter the United States; Washington had offered to lower that rate to 15% as part of a broader deal, but refuses to cut tariffs on medium and heavy trucks, according to the Globe and Mail [5].

In Cambodia, he added that if Canadian factories and workers are not “fully utilized within a North American framework, that opens up other possibilities,” and that “Canada will move forward regardless” [1][3].
Asked whether this was leverage against Washington, he replied: “It's not leverage.” Any Chinese investment would have to create real production in Canada, not just assemble imported parts [1].
Since the January agreement with Beijing, Canada has cut its tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles from 100% to 6.1%, for 49,000 vehicles a year at first, a quota set to grow [1].
